Here's what I did. First, I gave everyone one shared goal: reduce machine downtime. Everyone could see why the handoffs mattered. Second, I put all four teams on one plan, so every handoff was visible to everyone. Third, we kept one shared risk list with Philips, with an owner and a date for every dependency, and we reviewed it every week. And fourth, I used agreements instead of authority. We signed a data agreement with the Philips engineers on what data, in what format and how often. And the data and AI teams signed off integration together.
The result? The program passed all three stage gates on one plan, and problems came up in weekly reviews, not at the end.
So for me, when everyone sees the same plan, people hold themselves to it. You don't need authority.
Likely follow-up: "What if a team still doesn't deliver?"
Then I go to the person who manages that team, with the facts, the date we needed it and the cost of the delay. For vendors, it's in the contract.

q: Executive stakeholder conflict: two senior stakeholders have conflicting priorities, and both consider their requirements business-critical. How would you align them and reach a decision? (Similar to a follow-up in question 15)
a:
When two senior people both say their need is the most important, I don't pick a winner myself. I find out what each one really needs, I put the facts side by side, and I let the right person decide.
Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, my projects share the same engineers. When PaySFT lost half its team, the PaySFT side wanted more people urgently to save their launch. But Zolvit, a live platform, needed its full support team to keep the service running. Both said their need was critical.
Here's what I did. First, I spoke to each side to understand the real need. Zolvit needed the live service to keep running. PaySFT needed a launch date they could trust. So the fight was about people, not about goals. Second, I put both options side by side, showing what each choice would cost and what it would risk. Third, I kept Zolvit's support team where it was, because a live service always comes before a new build. And I gave the PaySFT client a clear, costed option of ₹32 lakh to deliver everything, so they could decide with the facts. And fourth, I wrote the decision down, so nobody opened it again later.
In the end, PaySFT delivered 125 APIs and two apps in 45 days, and Zolvit's service was never affected.
So for me, priority comes from business value, not from who is the most senior or who shouts the loudest.
Likely follow-up: "What if they still can't agree?"
Then I take both options to the person they both report to, with my recommendation. I don't decide it in the corridor.

q: How do you manage resource allocation when multiple projects require the same critical team members? (Similar to a follow-up in question 15)
a:
I protect what can't move, use an agreed rule for everything else, and when there's a real trade-off, the business decides with the facts. I never quietly take people from one project to save another.
Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, my projects share the same engineers. When PaySFT lost half its team, it needed people urgently. But Zolvit, a live platform, still needed its full support team.
Here's what I did. First, I didn't touch Zolvit's support team, because a live service always comes before a new build. Second, I re-planned PaySFT around the team it had, focusing on what was really needed for launch. Third, I gave the PaySFT client a clear, costed option of ₹32 lakh, instead of quietly pulling people from other projects. And fourth, for the longer term, I keep one view of everyone's capacity with rare skills flagged, and I train people across skills, so we don't depend on one person.
The result? PaySFT delivered 125 APIs and two apps in 45 days, and Zolvit's service was never affected.
So for me, priority comes from business value and commitments, not from whoever shouts the loudest.
Likely follow-up: "What if two leaders both say their project comes first?"
I put both options side by side, with the cost of delay, and take it to the leader they both report to, with my recommendation.

q: A product launch date is fixed but the scope is uncertain. How do you manage it? (Similar to question 16)
a:
If the date can't move, then the scope has to be flexible. So I agree the must-haves for the date early, build those first, and plan everything else as a later phase.
Let me give you an example. At Jazeera Airport, we were building a digital twin of the terminal, and the launch was tied to a leadership event, so the date could not move. Close to launch, live camera feeds for some zones were blocked by security approvals outside our control.
Here's what I did. First, we checked readiness against a clear go/no-go checklist, signed by each lead, so "nearly ready" turned into a clear list of what was red. Second, I gave the sponsor options with my recommendation: launch the ready zones live on the date, with clearly labelled recorded video for the rest. Third, the sponsor accepted the risk in writing, and we did two full rehearsals with a fallback. And fourth, I escalated the blocked approval through the client's IT head, with a clear date.
The result? The launch went ahead on the date without issues, and the remaining zones went live a few weeks later.
So for me, don't fight the date. Change what goes live on the date, and get the decision in writing.
Likely follow-up: "How do you decide what the must-haves are?"
With the sponsor, against the business goal of the launch. Anything that isn't needed for that goal on day one goes into phase two.

q: What approach do you follow to manage client expectations and maintain long-term client relationships? (Similar to a follow-up in question 18)
a:
For me, it's three simple things: agree expectations clearly at the start, no surprises along the way, and bring the client value beyond the contract. Long-term relationships come from helping with the client's next problem, not just this one.
Let me give you an example. At DP World, we worked with the operations team for a long time. The relationship was strong, but over time, expectations could drift.
Here's what I did. First, at the start, we agreed what success looks like, how we would work, and how we would handle changes. Second, I always shared bad news early, with options and my recommendation. Third, when the client sent quick informal requests, I gave them clear options and set up a weekly slot for small changes, so goodwill didn't turn into hidden extra work. And fourth, our leadership meetings focused on the client's business, not just on our status.
The result? Those meetings became the place where new business problems came up, and the relationship grew into four new projects.
So for me, keep the goodwill, but keep the promises clear and visible.
Likely follow-up: "How do you handle an unhappy client?"
I listen first, I own our part openly, and I agree a short recovery plan with clear checkpoints. Trust comes back through results, not words.

q: How do you manage scope changes when a client requests additional features during an ongoing project? (Similar to a follow-up in question 20)
a:
I never just say no, and I never quietly do the extra work for free. I look at the impact, give the client clear options, and make sure the decision is written down.
Let me give you an example. At DP World, the operations team got used to sending quick requests on WhatsApp or by phone, outside the agreed plan.
Here's what I did. First, I checked every request against the scope, the team's time and the plan. Second, I gave the client options: swap it for something of the same size, deliver a smaller version first, or add more people through a paid change request. Whatever they chose, we confirmed it in writing. And third, I made it a system: a weekly slot for quick changes, and one list for all requests, in priority order.
The result? The client still got their quick changes, just planned ones. The hidden weekend work stopped, and the relationship grew into four new projects.
So for me, scope changes are normal. It's unmanaged scope changes that break projects.
Likely follow-up: "What if the client says it was always in scope?"
We check the agreed scope together. If it's unclear, we agree a fair split, and we fix the wording for the future.

q: Commercial accountability: a project is delivering successfully from a technical perspective, but its costs are exceeding the approved budget. How would you manage financial performance while protecting business outcomes? (Similar to a follow-up in question 22)
a:
If a project is working well but costing too much, the problem is usually hidden somewhere, like rework or unpaid extra work. So I find out exactly where the money is going and fix that first, without hurting what the client actually cares about.
Let me give you an example. At Deluxe, I ran technology delivery for big Hollywood films like Black Panther and Thor: Ragnarok. We were meeting every deadline, and the work was great. But costs were about 18% over plan.
Here's what I did. First, I looked for where the money was going. I started tracking how much work the studio approved the first time. It turned out about 35% of our effort was going into redoing work after studio review. Second, I built quality in. We added our own review before anything went to the studio, and a short checklist to clear doubts before work started. Third, I invested in people and in automation. I coached the team and automated the repeated steps. And fourth, I stopped the leaks. I put three vendor schedules into one plan to cut waiting time, and I made sure every studio change was recorded, so we could bill for it.
The result? Productivity went up 20%, first-time approval went from about 60% to about 80%, and costs came back to within 5% of plan. And the studios were happier.
So for me, cutting quality to save money is the most expensive mistake you can make.
Likely follow-up: "What if you still can't close the gap?"
Then I tell the sponsor early, with a clear forecast, and give them a simple choice: more budget, less scope, or more time.

q: Predictability and risk forecasting: which delivery metrics would you use to predict future outcomes rather than simply report historical performance? How would you turn those insights into executive-level decisions? (Similar to a follow-up in question 23)
a:
Most reports tell you what already happened. I want numbers that tell me what is going to happen, so we have time to fix it. And every warning sign should come with a decision I need from leadership.
Let me give you an example. At Discreet Arts, leaders only found out about delays on the delivery day. At Hornbill, people said things had improved, but nobody could prove it.
Here's what I did. First, at Hornbill, I measured how long work took before changing anything, so we had a starting point. Second, I watched early warning signs: what we promised versus what we actually delivered, whether the scope was growing faster than the work being done, how long risks stayed open, and whether bugs were going up. Third, at Discreet Arts, I built a dashboard that turned amber as soon as a team started falling behind. And fourth, I didn't give leaders a single date. I gave them a likely range, and every amber item came with the decision I needed, like dropping some scope, adding people or moving a date.
The result? At Discreet Arts, we saw delays two to three weeks earlier. At Hornbill, delivery time came down by about 30%, and we could prove it.
So for me, looking back tells you what went wrong. Looking ahead gives you time to fix it.
Likely follow-up: "If you could track only one number?"
What we promised versus what we delivered. If that number starts dropping, the next milestone is in trouble.

q: How do you improve predictability without converting Agile teams into Waterfall teams? (Similar to a follow-up in question 23)
a:
Predictability doesn't come from big upfront plans. It comes from stable teams, small pieces of work, limits on work in progress, and forecasts based on real data.
Let me give you an example. At Hornbill, people said things had improved, but nobody could prove it, and delivery dates kept slipping. At Discreet Arts, leaders found out about delays only on the delivery day.
Here's what I did. First, at Hornbill, I measured how long work actually took before changing anything. Second, we limited how much work ran at the same time and broke work into smaller pieces, so it flowed faster and more evenly. Third, I tracked what we promised versus what we delivered, sprint by sprint. And fourth, at Discreet Arts, I built a dashboard that turned amber as soon as a team started falling behind, so we could act early, without adding heavy plans or approvals.
The result? At Hornbill, delivery time dropped by about 30%. At Discreet Arts, we saw delays two to three weeks earlier.
So for me, Agile teams become predictable when you measure the flow, not when you add more paperwork.
Likely follow-up: "How do you give leadership a date without a Waterfall plan?"
I use the team's real delivery data to give a likely range, and I update it every sprint as we learn more.

q: How do you identify and manage delivery risks before they affect project outcomes? (Similar to a follow-up in question 24)
a:
I look for early warning signs, not late results. Every big risk gets an owner, a plan, and a clear trigger that tells us when to act.
Let me give you an example. On the Philips project, early on, our software team built the system based on guesses about the machine data. When the real data arrived, it didn't match. And at Discreet Arts, leaders only found out about delays on the delivery day.
Here's what I did. First, after the Philips lesson, I made a signed data agreement a day-one task on every project. Second, I watch early warning signs: dependencies without dates, risks that stay open too long, a drop in what we deliver versus what we promised, and bugs going up. Third, at Discreet Arts, I built a dashboard that turned amber as soon as a team started falling behind. And fourth, I set clear time limits for escalation: to the program manager in 48 hours, to me in five days, and then to the steering committee.
The result? At Discreet Arts, we saw delays two to three weeks earlier. And on Philips, the program passed all three stage gates on one plan.
So for me, a risk list tells you what might happen. A trigger tells you when to act.
Likely follow-up: "Can you give an example of a trigger?"
Sure. "If the vendor's integration isn't in testing by the 15th, we switch to the backup and escalate to their account director." It's specific, it has a date, and someone owns it.

q: Vendor performance crisis: a strategic vendor fails to meet critical milestones, putting a major product launch at risk. How would you manage contractual obligations, recovery planning and stakeholder communication? (Similar to a follow-up in question 25)
a:
When a key vendor misses deadlines, I do four things at the same time: protect our position in the contract, push the vendor to recover, prepare a backup, and make sure the sponsor hears it from me first. The goal is to save the launch, not to win the argument.
Let me give you an example. At Deluxe, several vendors worked on the same film projects, and every release date was fixed. Vendor handoffs started slipping and turning into arguments, and that put studio deadlines at risk.
Here's what I did. First, I settled every dispute using the contract and the agreed scope, not opinions. So each vendor knew exactly what they owed and by when. Second, I put all three vendor schedules into one recovery plan, with owners and dates, and tracked it closely. Third, I asked vendor teams to follow the same quality checks as our own team. And fourth, I made sure the studio and our leadership heard about any risk from me first, with the impact and the plan.
The result? We met every studio deadline, and the combined plan also helped bring costs back to within 5% of plan.
So for me, you handle vendor problems with facts, the contract and a backup plan, and never with surprises for the sponsor.
Likely follow-up: "What if the vendor still can't recover?"
Then I use the remedies in the contract and switch to the backup I prepared, like another vendor or doing the work in-house. Today, at NeuSix, I put reporting rules into vendor contracts from day one.

q: How do you measure AI in delivery? (Similar to question 28)
a:
I measure AI at four levels: is it accurate, is it used, what does it cost, and does it move a business number. If I only measure the model, I'm measuring a demo, not delivery.
I've delivered AI on Zolvit, Vigilant and the Philips digital twin, and this is the scorecard I use.
First, quality: before go-live, the AI is scored against an agreed test set. On Zolvit, that was real legal questions with answers agreed by legal experts. After go-live, I track accuracy in real use and how often a person has to correct it. Second, adoption: how many users actually rely on it, and how often they accept its output versus override it. Third, cost and control: cost per task and time taken. On Vigilant, we logged every agent action and the cost of each task from day one. And finally, business outcome: the client's own number, such as hours saved, faster responses or new sales pipeline, measured against a baseline taken before the AI went in.
When the question is about AI tools used by my own team, like Copilot, I apply the same rule as at Hornbill: baseline first, then speed and quality together, meaning cycle time, defects that reach the client, rework and code-review time. Faster work with more defects doesn't count.
On Vigilant, agents went live only after passing the agreed score, with accuracy above X% and cost per task tracked from day one.
In short, if you don't measure before, you can't prove anything after.
Likely follow-up: "Which of the four matters most to a CXO?"
The business outcome. But I report all four, because the other three explain why the outcome is or isn't moving.

q: What steps do you take to improve delivery efficiency and reduce operational costs without compromising quality? (Similar to a follow-up in question 60)
a:
I measure first, then remove waste, and I always check quality at the same time. Most of the cost is hidden in rework and waiting, not in people.
Let me give you two examples. At Hornbill, delivery was slow, and people said things had improved, but nobody could prove it. At Deluxe, we met every film deadline, but costs were about 18% over plan.
Here's what I did. First, at Hornbill, I measured how long work took before changing anything. Second, I removed waste: one priority list, one way to bring in requests, and a limit on how much work runs at the same time. Third, at Deluxe, I cut rework. We tracked how much work was approved the first time, and added our own review before anything went to the studio. And fourth, we automated the repeated steps and put three vendor schedules into one plan to cut waiting time.
The result? At Hornbill, delivery time dropped by about 30%, and we could prove it. At Deluxe, productivity went up 20%, costs came back to within 5% of plan, and the studios were happier.
So for me, cutting quality to save money is the most expensive mistake you can make.
Likely follow-up: "Where do you look first?"
Rework and waiting time, because they cost the most, and fixing them improves quality at the same time.

q: Can you take me through the technical architecture of one of your projects? (Similar to question 62)
a:
Let me take you from the user's phone to the database and back, then cover security, DevOps and how it scales. I'll use PaySFT, the real-estate platform where we delivered 125 APIs and two mobile apps in 45 days.
First, users and channels: Broker and Buyer mobile apps, plus a web admin portal, built with React Native or Flutter for mobile and React for web. Second, edge: traffic comes through a CDN and firewall, then an API gateway that checks logins, applies rate limits and routes requests. Users sign in through an identity service such as Cognito or Auth0. Third, application layer: the 125 APIs are grouped into services by business area, such as listings, users, leads, payments and notifications, so each can be built, deployed and scaled separately, running as Node.js or Java services in containers. Fourth, data layer: a relational database for core transactions (PostgreSQL), a cache for speed (Redis), search for property listings (Elasticsearch), and object storage for images and documents (S3). Fifth, integration: a message queue (SQS or Kafka), so slow tasks like notifications and third-party calls don't hold up the user, with external services for payments, maps, SMS and email. And finally, AI layer, where relevant: on Vigilant and Zolvit, the AI sits behind its own service, with guardrails, evaluation and cost logging, so the AI can change without touching the rest.
Across all layers: infrastructure defined as code (Terraform), a CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions) with automated tests and security scans on every change, and separate dev, test and production environments. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest, with role-based access, secrets in a vault and audit logs. Every service has logs, metrics and alerts (CloudWatch or Grafana). Services scale automatically with load, and the system runs across multiple availability zones with backups and a tested recovery plan.
My delivery angle: we agreed the API contracts first, so the mobile and backend teams could build in parallel, which is a big reason we hit 45 days. Every interface had an owner, we tested integration every sprint, and targets like response time and uptime were agreed up front and checked before go-live.
I don't need to write the code, but I need to understand the architecture well enough to see where the risk is. On PaySFT, that was the API contracts between mobile and backend, so that's where I put the most control.
Likely follow-up: "Why microservices and not a monolith?"
For PaySFT, separate services let small teams work in parallel and scale the busy parts, like listings and search, independently. For a small, simple app, I'd start with a well-structured single application and split it later, because microservices add running cost.

q: How do you report Agile delivery status to non-Agile executives? (Similar to question 71)
a:
Executives don't need to learn Agile. So I translate sprint progress into the things they care about: dates, money, risks and the decisions I need from them, on one page.
Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I run steering meetings with CEO-level sponsors. They didn't want to hear about story points or velocity. They wanted to know: are we on track, what's at risk, and what do you need from me?
Here's what I do. First, I report in milestones and business results, not sprints. For example, "the payments feature is live" instead of "we finished sprint 7". Second, I give a forecast range based on real data, like "most likely mid-March, latest end of March", instead of one date I can't trust. Third, red, amber and green follow clear written rules, so the colour isn't my opinion. And fourth, every red or amber item comes with options and the decision I need, and the pack goes out two days before the meeting.
The result? Steering meetings became short and decision-focused. And at DP World, those meetings became the place where new business problems came up, which led to four new projects.
So for me, Agile is how the team works. The executive report should speak the business's language.
Likely follow-up: "What if an executive wants a fixed date for everything?"
I give them a date for what's committed and a range for the rest, and I explain what would make the date move.

q: Value versus velocity: your teams consistently meet sprint commitments, yet business stakeholders report that delivery isn't generating the expected value. How would you identify and address the underlying problem? (Similar to question 78)
a:
If the team is hitting its sprint goals but the business isn't happy, it usually means we are building the wrong things very well. So I stop measuring how much we deliver, and start measuring what difference it makes to the business.
Let me give you an example. At DP World, the team was delivering, but the business couldn't see the value.
Here's what I did. First, we went to the real users, the people doing the work every day, and asked them what problem they needed solved, and what they actually saw from our releases. Second, every piece of work had to link to a real business problem, with a measure the business agreed. If it didn't link to anything, it went down the list. Third, I changed what we reported. Velocity stayed inside the team for planning, and the leadership meetings focused on business results. And fourth, we showed our work to real users regularly, so we got feedback every sprint, not at the end.
The result? Bringing in the real users turned the program around, and it led to four new projects, each with its own business case.
So for me, velocity tells you the team is busy. Only business results tell you the business is better off.
Likely follow-up: "What if the product owner says the backlog is right?"
I don't argue opinions. I bring the usage data and the measure we agreed, and we look at it together with the sponsor. The data usually settles it.

q: Leadership under pressure: a high-performing delivery lead repeatedly misses commitments and blames external dependencies. How would you investigate the issue, establish accountability and improve performance? (Similar to question 79)
a:
When a good lead keeps missing commitments and blames others, I first check the facts before I judge the person. Sometimes the dependencies really are the problem. Sometimes they are just the excuse. Either way, the lead is still responsible for managing them.
Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, I was brought in for six months because several projects were missing deadlines. The leads were good people, and every delay seemed to have a reason outside their team.
Here's what I did. First, I looked at the facts. I went through every project's plan and risks. Most delays came from risks that were known for weeks, but nobody owned them and nobody had a date. Second, I had honest, private conversations. I showed each lead how one risk, left open for weeks, had turned into the exact delay we were facing. Facts, not blame. Good people respond well to that. Third, I made ownership clear. We had one risk list with a name and a date on every item, and a clear rule: if you depend on someone else, it's still your job to track it and raise it early. And fourth, where the problem really was outside their control, like people being moved between projects every day, I fixed it myself with one staffing plan.
The result? The leads started owning their risks. By day 60, leadership had one view they trusted, and by day 90, we were tracking weekly results.
So for me, you can't control every dependency, but you can always control how early you see it and how fast you raise it.
Likely follow-up: "What if they still don't improve?"
After a fair and documented period of support, I would start a formal performance process with HR. Being good in the past earns patience, not an exemption.

q: Governance transformation: you join an organisation where delivery governance involves excessive reporting, frequent status meetings and slow decision-making. What changes would you introduce without losing executive visibility or control? (Similar to question 80)
a:
Governance should make decisions faster, not slower. So I keep leadership's visibility, but I change how they get it: live data instead of manual reports, and short meetings that only look at problems and decisions.
Let me give you an example. At Discreet Arts, leaders often found out about problems only on the delivery day. At NeuSix, people were putting together status reports by hand, across our teams and four vendors.
Here's what I did. First, at NeuSix, I made Jira and Confluence the one place for all project information, so nobody had to build reports by hand. Second, at Discreet Arts, I built a simple dashboard that turned amber when a team started falling behind. So leaders saw problems early. Third, leadership meetings only covered red and amber items and the decisions needed, and the pack went out two days before. And fourth, I made it clear who decides what: the team, the program manager, me or the steering committee. And the rule was, decide or escalate within 48 hours.
The result? At Discreet Arts, we saw delays two to three weeks earlier, and leadership meetings became short problem reviews. At NeuSix, we got one view across all projects and vendors.
So for me, leaders don't want more reports. They want no surprises and quick decisions.
Likely follow-up: "How do you make the change without leaders feeling they've lost control?"
I run the new dashboard next to the old reports for a month. Once they trust it, we switch the old reports off.

q: Strategic leadership: your organisation must deliver a major transformation within six months, but resources are limited and priorities keep changing. How would you build a realistic delivery strategy, prioritise initiatives and ensure sustainable execution? (Similar to question 81)
a:
When you have six months, not enough people and priorities keep changing, the plan has to expect change. So I focus on a few big results, put our people on what matters most, and handle new priorities in a controlled way.
Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, I was given six months to fix several projects that were in trouble. There was no budget for more people, people were being moved between projects every day, and priorities kept changing.
Here's what I did. First, I didn't jump in. I looked at every project, its goals, its people, its money and its delivery, to find the real problems. Second, I made one staffing plan for all projects, so people stopped being moved every day, and I put my strongest leads on the most important projects. Third, I set up one risk list with owners and a clear escalation path. So any change in priority became a clear decision with an owner, not a daily surprise. And fourth, I worked in steps, at 30, 60 and 90 days, with a visible result at each step, so leadership and the team could see progress.
The result? By day 30, we knew where every project stood. By day 60, leadership had one view they trusted. And by day 90, we were tracking weekly results. Delivery became predictable again.
So for me, in six months you can't do everything. The real strategy is deciding what not to do, and saying it early.
Likely follow-up: "What if leadership keeps adding priorities?"
I show them on one page what the new item will push out, and how much time it costs. The sponsor decides, and we write it down.

q: How do you deliver a roadmap when product priorities change every month? (Similar to question 81)
a:
When priorities change every month, I stop planning in fixed long lists and plan around outcomes instead. The goals stay steady, and the detailed list is reviewed at a set time each month.
Let me give you an example. At Hornbill, requests came in from everywhere, priorities kept changing, and delivery was slow.
Here's what I did. First, I put everything into one priority list, with one way for requests to come in, so changes came through one door. Second, the roadmap showed goals for each quarter, and only the next few weeks were planned in detail. Third, priority changes were reviewed once a month at a fixed meeting, not every day, and anything new had to push something else out. And fourth, I limited how much work ran at the same time, so the team could finish things before the next change came.
The result? Delivery time came down by about 30%, and we could prove it against our starting point.
So for me, change is normal. The trick is to handle it at a fixed time, through one door.
Likely follow-up: "What if a senior leader wants a change right now?"
I show them what it pushes out and what it costs. If it's truly urgent, the sponsor decides, and we write it down.

q: How do you handle disagreements between technical teams and business stakeholders about delivery priorities? (Similar to question 82)
a:
I don't take sides. I turn the disagreement into a clear trade-off that both sides can see, and I agree a simple rule, so we don't have the same argument every sprint.
Let me give you an example. On Zolvit, a live legal platform, the business wanted new features as fast as possible. The tech team wanted time to keep the system stable and fix the causes of support problems. Both were right, and we had the same argument at every planning meeting.
Here's what I did. First, I asked both sides to make their case clearly. The business showed why each feature mattered, and the tech team showed the risk to the service if we skipped stability work. Second, we agreed a rule. A fixed part of the team's time was kept for keeping the service running, and about 10% for improvements. So support and new features stopped competing. Third, within the feature time, the business decided the order, and the tech team raised risks openly. And fourth, we reviewed the split regularly, so either side could ask to change it, with facts.
The result? Zolvit's service stayed stable, improvements kept coming, and planning stopped being a fight.
So for me, most arguments about priorities end when both sides agree the rule before they argue the case.
Likely follow-up: "What if they still disagree on one item?"
I take both options, with the cost and the risk, to the sponsor with my recommendation, and we write the decision down.

q: How do you measure team performance and ensure accountability across different project teams? (Similar to question 83)
a:
I measure every team with the same small set of numbers: speed, quality and keeping promises. And I make it clear who owns what, with names and dates, instead of using pressure.
Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I run five programs. Every lead used to report progress in their own way, so it was hard to compare teams or spot problems early.
Here's what I did. First, I set one simple scorecard for every team: what we promised versus what we delivered, how long work takes, bugs that reach the client, and risks that are overdue. Second, I always measure speed and quality together. At Deluxe, we tracked productivity and rework side by side, so nobody could look fast by shipping bugs. Third, I keep one risk list in Jira and Confluence across all programs, with a name and a date on every item. And fourth, I use the numbers to coach, not to punish. And I always take a starting measurement first, like at Hornbill, so improvement is proven, not just claimed.
The result? At Hornbill, delivery time dropped by about 30%. At Deluxe, productivity went up 20%. And at NeuSix, I can now see a team slipping within days, not at the deadline.
So for me, accountability is easy when everyone can see the same facts and the same rules apply to every team.
Likely follow-up: "How do you stop teams gaming the numbers?"
Every speed number is paired with a quality number, and the numbers are used to ask questions, not to blame people.

q: Can you describe how you would handle a major production issue immediately after a project release while ensuring minimal business disruption? (Similar to question 84)
a:
First, get the service back up. Then find the cause. Then make sure it doesn't happen again. And while it's happening, the business hears from me early and often, with facts, not guesses.
Let me give you an example of how I prepare for this. On Zolvit, a live legal platform, an outage is a serious risk for the client's reputation. So I made sure the team was ready before anything went wrong.
Here's how I handle it. First, I prepare before the release: a tested rollback plan, monitoring and alerts, step-by-step guides, and we practise the most likely problems in advance. Second, when a big issue happens, one person leads the response, we check the business impact, and if rolling back is the fastest way to fix it, we roll back. The root cause can wait; the business can't. Third, I keep the client informed: the sponsor hears from me within the hour, then I give regular updates, say every 30 minutes, until it's fixed. And fourth, within a few days, we hold a no-blame review, fix the root cause, and add the lesson to our tests and release checklist.
The result? Zolvit's service stayed stable, and every big issue made our process better. I use the same thinking in the support period after every go-live, like at Jazeera Airport, where we launched on time, in phases.
So for me, in an incident, getting the service back and keeping people informed matter much more than finding someone to blame.
Likely follow-up: "Would you roll back or fix forward?"
Roll back by default, if it's the fastest safe way to restore the service. I only fix forward if the fix is small, tested and quicker than a rollback.
